why_how.text: The Class C privilege has a set scope, and the application has a list of requirements you must meet.
Ages and signatures are exact rules, especially for applicants under eighteen.

scenario.text: A seventeen-year-old applies for a license, and the parent cannot come to DMV.

reasoning.text: An applicant under eighteen needs a parent or legal guardian to sign the electronic application, or to sign a separate form if that adult cannot come to DMV.

result.text: The parent signs the separate form, and the application goes forward.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the permit age and the license age are the same.

correction.text: The instruction permit age is fifteen, while the driver license age is sixteen.

memory_support.text: Permit at fifteen, license at sixteen.

prompt.text: What is the youngest age at which you may apply for an Oregon driver license?

rationale.text: You must be at least sixteen years old to apply for a driver license, while the instruction permit age is fifteen.

lines.text: What you must do to apply.

narration.text: This lesson covers the Class C non-commercial driving privilege: what it lets you drive, how old you must be, and everything you need to apply. A Class C non-commercial driving privilege lets you drive a passenger car, moped, autocycle, van or pickup weighing no more than twenty-six thousand pounds that does not require a commercial driver license or a motorcycle endorsement. To get it, you meet age rules, complete an application with the right signatures and proof, pass tests and pay fees, and follow the photo rules. We will go through each requirement in turn.

There are two minimum ages. You must be at least fifteen years old to apply for an instruction permit. You must be at least sixteen years old to apply for a driver license. So the instruction permit age is fifteen, while the driver license age is sixteen. The permit comes first, and for applicants under eighteen the permit also starts a required holding period that the next lesson covers. Keep the two numbers paired with the right document: fifteen goes with the permit, and sixteen goes with the license. Keep that rule in mind.

You apply with an electronic application. An applicant under eighteen needs a parent or legal guardian to sign it, or to sign a separate form if that adult cannot come to DMV. An applicant who is emancipated or married shows proof of that status and then needs no parent or guardian signature. Every applicant must present proof of identity, date of birth and residence address. And you must provide your Social Security Number or certify electronically that you do not have one. Each of these is a separate requirement on the application.

A first-time applicant under eighteen needs a parent or guardian to certify school enrollment or attendance, or, if no longer in school, must show a high school diploma or GED certificate. To get the privilege you must pass the required knowledge, vision and drive tests and pay the applicable fees. So a teen applicant adds a school requirement on top of the parent signature, and every applicant takes the same three tests and pays the fees. Passing the tests and paying the fees are both needed before the privilege is issued.

lines.text: Fifteen is not the license age.
Sixteen is not the permit age.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Learners swap the two ages, or merge them into one. The instruction permit age is fifteen, while the driver license age is sixteen. So a fifteen-year-old may apply for a permit but not for a license, and a sixteen-year-old may apply for a license. Under eighteen, a parent or legal guardian signs the application, unless the applicant is emancipated or married and shows proof of that status. Pair each age with its document and each applicant type with its signature rule, and this topic becomes straightforward.

Here is a quick check: what is the youngest age at which you may apply for an Oregon driver license? The answer is sixteen. You must be at least sixteen years old to apply for a driver license. The instruction permit comes earlier, at fifteen. If you mixed those up, go back to the pairing: fifteen goes with the instruction permit, and sixteen goes with the driver license. And remember that an applicant under eighteen also needs a parent or legal guardian signature, unless emancipated or married with proof. Keep that rule in mind.

lines.text: Photo: no hats, glasses or face paint.

narration.text: Two last requirements finish the application. For the license photo, hats, glasses, face paint or other temporary substances on the face, and contact lenses that change how the eye looks, are not allowed. And you cannot be under suspension, revocation or cancellation in Oregon or any other state, and you must surrender any other driving privilege or ID card. Together with the ages, the signature rules, proof of identity, birth date and address, your Social Security Number, the school rule for teens, the tests and the fees, that is the full list.

why_how.text: Applicants under eighteen must meet a permit period and a practice requirement before getting a license.
Practice only counts with a qualified supervisor.

scenario.text: A sixteen-year-old has held a permit for more than six months, completed an ODOT-approved traffic safety course, and logged fifty supervised hours with a parent who is over twenty-one and has been licensed for more than three years.

reasoning.text: The permit was held at least six months, fifty hours plus an approved course meets the practice rule, and the supervisor is over twenty-one with more than three years of driving privileges.

result.text: The practice and permit requirements are met, as long as DMV receives proof of the course completion.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking every teen must log one hundred supervised hours.

correction.text: A teen meets the practice requirement either with one hundred supervised hours alone, or with fifty hours plus an ODOT-approved traffic safety education course.

memory_support.text: Six months held, one hundred hours or fifty plus a course.

prompt.text: How long must an applicant under eighteen hold an instruction permit before getting a license?

rationale.text: An applicant under eighteen must have held an instruction permit for at least six months, and time on an out-of-state permit counts.

narration.text: Applicants under eighteen have extra requirements before they can get a driver license. There are three: how long they must hold an instruction permit, how many hours of supervised driving they need, and who may supervise those hours. Each rule comes with an exact number. This lesson goes through them one by one and then compares the two ways to meet the practice requirement, because that choice between an hours-only path and a course path is where most confusion happens. All of these rules apply only to applicants under eighteen.

lines.text: Hold the permit at least six months.
One hundred hours, or fifty plus a course.

narration.text: An applicant under eighteen must have held an instruction permit for at least six months before getting a license, and time on an out-of-state permit counts. The same applicant needs one hundred hours of supervised driving, or fifty hours plus an ODOT-approved traffic safety education course whose completion proof DMV must receive. So there are two paths for practice: one hundred supervised hours alone, or fifty supervised hours combined with an approved course. On the course path, DMV must receive proof that the course was completed.

Supervised practice counts only when the supervisor is at least twenty-one years old and has held valid driving privileges for at least three years. Both conditions must be true. A supervisor who is twenty-one but has been licensed for only two years does not qualify, and neither does someone licensed for many years who is under twenty-one. So the teen permit must be held at least six months, while the practice supervisor must be at least twenty-one and licensed for at least three years. Those are two separate rules with separate numbers.

lines.text: Fifty plus a course also works.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many learners believe every teen must log one hundred supervised hours. That is only one of two paths. A teen applicant reaches the practice requirement either with one hundred supervised hours alone, or with fifty supervised hours combined with an ODOT-approved traffic safety education course, whose completion proof DMV must receive. So taking an approved course cuts the required hours to fifty. Either path also needs a qualified supervisor, at least twenty-one with at least three years of valid driving privileges, for the hours to count.

Here is a quick check: an applicant under eighteen wants a driver license. How long must they have held an instruction permit first? The answer is at least six months. And time spent on an out-of-state permit counts toward those six months. The other two teen rules come with their own numbers: one hundred supervised hours, or fifty plus an approved course, and a supervisor who is at least twenty-one and has held valid driving privileges for at least three years. Keep the six months tied to the permit. Keep that rule in mind.

lines.text: One hundred hours, or fifty plus a course.

narration.text: To finish: an applicant under eighteen must hold an instruction permit for at least six months, and out-of-state permit time counts. They need one hundred hours of supervised driving, or fifty hours plus an ODOT-approved traffic safety education course with completion proof sent to DMV. And the hours count only when the supervisor is at least twenty-one years old and has held valid driving privileges for at least three years. Those three rules, together with the ages and the parent signature from the last lesson, cover every teen requirement.

why_how.text: DMV accepts only certain documents as proof, and many of them have expiry windows.
Address proof has its own list, including what does not count.

scenario.text: An applicant brings an Oregon ID card that expired less than thirteen years ago and a utility bill showing their address.

reasoning.text: An Oregon driver license, permit or ID card is accepted if valid or expired no more than thirteen years, and a utility bill can prove the address.

result.text: Both documents are accepted: the ID card expired less than thirteen years ago and one address document is enough.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking any personal letter mailed to your home proves your address.

correction.text: Mail from a business, school or government agency showing your first and last name proves your address, but personal mail and forwarded mail do not.

memory_support.text: Thirteen years for Oregon, one year from out of state.

prompt.text: An out-of-state license expired more than one year ago. Can it be used as proof?

rationale.text: An out-of-state driver license, permit or ID card is accepted only if valid or expired no more than one year.

narration.text: Every applicant must prove identity, date of birth and residence address. This lesson covers which documents count. Documents used as proof of identity and date of birth must be originals or certified copies from the agency that issued them. Many accepted documents can be used even after they expire, but only within a set window, and those windows differ by document. After identity, we turn to name changes and then to the separate list of documents that prove your residence address, including two kinds of mail that do not count at all.

A U.S. government-issued birth certificate is accepted proof, but hospital-issued birth certificates and baptismal records are not. A DMV-approved tribal ID card from a federally recognized tribe located in Oregon is accepted, as is a Certificate of Naturalization or Certificate of Citizenship. Remember that each of these must be an original or a certified copy from the agency that issued it. Keep the birth certificate rule exact: government-issued is accepted, while hospital-issued certificates and baptismal records are not.

Several documents are accepted if they are valid or have been expired no more than five years. A U.S. passport or passport card falls in this group. So do an Employment Authorization Card, a Permanent Resident Card, a foreign passport, a Re-entry Permit and a Refugee Travel Document. A consulate card is also accepted if it is valid or has been expired no more than five years. So for every document in this group, an expired one still works as long as it expired five years ago or less, and not beyond that point. Keep that rule in mind.

Driver cards have their own windows. An Oregon driver license, permit or ID card is accepted as proof if valid or expired no more than thirteen years. An out-of-state driver license, permit or ID card is accepted only if valid or expired no more than one year. So an expired Oregon card can still prove identity for up to thirteen years after expiry, while an expired out-of-state card counts for only up to one year. And if your current legal name differs from the name on your identity document, you must also prove the legal name change.

lines.text: Check where the card is from.

narration.text: Here is the trap. A new Oregon resident brings an out-of-state license that expired more than one year ago, expecting the long thirteen-year window to apply. It does not. The thirteen-year window is only for an Oregon driver license, permit or ID card. An out-of-state driver license, permit or ID card is accepted only if valid or expired no more than one year. So before relying on an expired card, check two things: where it was issued, and how long ago it expired. The answer to both decides whether it counts. Keep that rule in mind.

One document is enough to prove your residence address when you apply. Someone who lives at your address can certify it, but that person must come with you and show proof of the address, such as their own license or ID card. Mail from a business, school or government agency showing your first and last name proves your address, but personal mail and forwarded mail do not. A document from an educational provider, a utility hookup order or bill, a mortgage document or a property tax statement can also prove your address. Keep that rule in mind.

Here is a quick check: an applicant brings an out-of-state driver license that expired more than one year ago. Can it be used as proof? The answer is no. An out-of-state driver license, permit or ID card is accepted only if valid or expired no more than one year, so it is past that window. If the same card had been issued by Oregon, it would be accepted, because an Oregon license, permit or ID card is accepted if valid or expired no more than thirteen years. Where the card was issued decides which window applies. Keep that rule in mind.

lines.text: Full lists on the DMV website.

narration.text: To wrap up: proof documents must be originals or certified copies from the issuing agency. A government-issued birth certificate counts, hospital certificates and baptismal records do not. Passports, immigration documents and consulate cards work up to five years after expiry, Oregon driver cards up to thirteen years, and out-of-state cards only up to one year. Prove any legal name change. One address document is enough, and personal or forwarded mail does not count. The full list of accepted documents is on the Oregon DMV website, and REAL ID requirements are on the state's REAL ID page.

why_how.text: Your card can carry donor, veteran or hearing designations, each with its own proof rule.
Oregon law sets minimum insurance amounts for each type of coverage.

scenario.text: A driver compares the minimum coverages on a new insurance policy.

reasoning.text: Oregon's minimum bodily injury coverage is twenty-five thousand dollars per collision for one person and fifty thousand for two or more, and the property damage minimum is twenty thousand dollars.

result.text: The policy meets the minimums only if it has at least those amounts, plus the Personal Injury Protection and Uninsured Motorist minimums.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a veteran designation needs no proof, like the hearing designation.

correction.text: A veteran designation requires a discharge document as proof, while a deaf or hard of hearing designation requires no proof at all.

prompt.text: What is Oregon's minimum property damage coverage per collision?

rationale.text: Oregon's minimum property damage coverage is twenty thousand dollars per collision for damage to other people's property.

narration.text: This lesson covers two topics. The first is the designations you can add to your license or permit: organ, eye and tissue donor, veteran, and deaf or hard of hearing. Each has its own rule about proof. The second is mandatory insurance, where Oregon law sets minimum amounts for bodily injury, property damage, Personal Injury Protection and Uninsured Motorist Coverage. The insurance amounts are exact dollar figures that are easy to mix up, so we will go through each one and then compare the ones that share or nearly share a number.

lines.text: Donor: heart on front, words on back.

narration.text: When you are issued a driving privilege you can join the organ, eye and tissue donor registry, and DMV adds a heart symbol to the front of the card and the words Anatomical Donor to the back. A veteran may ask for a veteran designation by showing a DD two fourteen or DD two fifteen form that shows discharge under honorable conditions. You may ask DMV to add a deaf or hard of hearing designation with no proof required, and it is also visible to law enforcement through your DMV record. Keep that rule in mind. That is the rule to remember.

Here is the trap. Because the deaf or hard of hearing designation needs no proof, learners assume the veteran designation works the same way. It does not. A veteran designation requires a discharge document as proof, a DD two fourteen or DD two fifteen form showing discharge under honorable conditions, while a deaf or hard of hearing designation requires no proof at all. So one designation is added on request alone, and the other requires a specific document. Match the designation to its proof rule before you answer. Keep that rule in mind.

lines.text: Bodily injury: twenty-five and fifty thousand.

narration.text: Oregon's minimum bodily injury coverage is twenty-five thousand dollars per collision for one person and fifty thousand dollars per collision for injury to or death of two or more people. Oregon's minimum property damage coverage is twenty thousand dollars per collision for damage to other people's property. So the minimum liability limits are twenty-five thousand dollars for injury to one person and fifty thousand for two or more people per collision, while the separate property damage minimum is twenty thousand dollars.

lines.text: Uninsured Motorist: twenty-five and fifty thousand.

narration.text: Personal Injury Protection must be at least fifteen thousand dollars per person for reasonable and necessary medical, dental and other expenses incurred within two years after the injury. Uninsured Motorist Coverage must be at least twenty-five thousand dollars per person and fifty thousand dollars per collision for bodily injury. So Personal Injury Protection is set at fifteen thousand dollars per person, while Uninsured Motorist Coverage is set at twenty-five thousand dollars per person and fifty thousand dollars per collision, the same pair of numbers as the bodily injury minimums.

Here is a quick check: what is Oregon's minimum property damage coverage per collision? The answer is twenty thousand dollars, for damage to other people's property. Do not confuse it with the bodily injury minimums of twenty-five thousand dollars for one person and fifty thousand for two or more, or with Personal Injury Protection, which is at least fifteen thousand dollars per person. Uninsured Motorist Coverage uses the same twenty-five thousand and fifty thousand dollar figures as bodily injury. Property damage alone is twenty thousand.

To finish: the donor registry adds a heart symbol to the front of your card and the words Anatomical Donor to the back, a veteran designation requires a DD two fourteen or DD two fifteen showing honorable discharge, and a deaf or hard of hearing designation needs no proof and is visible to law enforcement. For insurance, the minimums are twenty-five thousand and fifty thousand dollars for bodily injury, twenty thousand for property damage, fifteen thousand per person for Personal Injury Protection, and twenty-five thousand and fifty thousand for Uninsured Motorist Coverage.

why_how.text: After a collision the manual lists exact duties at the scene and exact triggers for a DMV report.
Keeping your privilege depends on your driving record, and some actions can cost it.

scenario.text: A driver backs into a fence and causes more than two thousand five hundred dollars of damage, and police are not called.

reasoning.text: Damage to property other than a vehicle over two thousand five hundred dollars requires a report within seventy-two hours, and the owner or person in charge of the property must be told.

result.text: The driver tells the property owner and files the collision report within seventy-two hours.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a police report at the scene takes care of the DMV report.

correction.text: A police report does not replace your duty to file your own collision report with DMV.

memory_support.text: Stop, help, swap, stay, report within seventy-two hours.

prompt.text: Someone is unconscious after a collision you were in. When may you leave the scene?

rationale.text: If anyone is killed or unconscious after a collision, you stay at the scene until police arrive.

lines.text: Duties at the scene and after.

narration.text: The manual calls the word accident misleading: a collision caused by being distracted, tired or not driving defensively is a preventable collision. This lesson covers what you must do if you are in one. First come the duties at the scene, including the one situation where you must stay until police arrive. Then come the triggers for filing a collision report with DMV, the deadline, and the rule about police reports. After that we cover unattended vehicles and other property, and finally what can cost you your driving privilege.

lines.text: Stop; clear lanes if no one is hurt.

narration.text: After a collision you must stop. If no one is hurt and the vehicles can be moved safely, get them out of the travel lanes quickly and swap information away from the scene. You must give reasonable help to anyone injured in a collision, and injured people should never be moved carelessly. Give your name, address, driver license number, vehicle plate number and insurance details to the other driver, passengers or any injured pedestrian involved. And if anyone is killed or unconscious after a collision, stay at the scene until police arrive.

lines.text: Damage over two thousand five hundred dollars.

narration.text: You must file a collision report on the DMV collision report form within seventy-two hours when damage to the vehicle you were driving is over two thousand five hundred dollars, or damage to property other than a vehicle is over two thousand five hundred dollars. A report is also required within seventy-two hours when any vehicle has more than two thousand five hundred dollars of damage and any vehicle is towed from the scene because of collision damage. And a report is required whenever the collision causes injury or death.

lines.text: A police report is not your report.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Police come to the scene and write a report, so the driver assumes the paperwork is done. It is not. A police report does not replace your duty to file your own collision report with DMV. The DMV report is due within seventy-two hours whenever one of the triggers is met. And if the driver of your vehicle fails to report a reportable collision, a vehicle owner must file the collision report. So check the triggers yourself and file your own report, whatever the police have done. Keep that rule in mind. That is the rule to remember.

lines.text: Find the owner or leave a note.
Tell whoever is in charge of property.

narration.text: If you hit an unoccupied vehicle, try to find its owner, and if you cannot, leave a note with your name, address and a short account of what happened. Damaging something that is not a motor vehicle carries the same duty: look for its owner or whoever is in charge of it and tell them about the damage. So hitting a parked car or a fence does not end with driving away. You find the owner or the person in charge, and for a vehicle you cannot match to an owner, you leave a note with the details the manual lists. Keep that rule in mind.

Keeping your driving privilege depends on keeping a good driving record. You can lose your driving privilege for driving under the influence of alcohol, drugs or inhalants, for failing to report a collision, or for driving uninsured. Too many traffic convictions, handled through the Driver Improvement Program, and failing to comply with court fines can also cost you your privilege. And the manual says its list is not complete. So the reasons named are examples, and the general rule is that your record decides whether you keep your privilege.

Here is a quick check: after a collision, one of the people involved is unconscious. When may you leave the scene? The answer is only after police arrive. If anyone is killed or unconscious after a collision, you stay at the scene until police arrive. That is different from a collision where no one is hurt and the vehicles can be moved safely, where you clear the travel lanes and swap information away from the scene. And in every collision, you give reasonable help to anyone injured without moving them carelessly. Keep that rule in mind.

lines.text: Stop, help, exchange, stay if needed.

narration.text: To wrap up: after a collision, stop, clear the lanes if no one is hurt, help anyone injured without moving them carelessly, exchange your name, address, license number, plate and insurance details, and stay until police arrive if anyone is killed or unconscious. File a DMV report within seventy-two hours for damage over two thousand five hundred dollars, towing with that damage, or any injury or death, even if police made a report. Find the owner of an unoccupied vehicle or leave a note, and remember that a good record keeps your privilege.
